{{Short description|Armenian-American chemist}}

[[File:Nerses Krikorian.gif|thumb|Nerses Krikorian]]
'''Nerses "Krik" Krikorian''' (January 1921{{spaced ndash}}April 18, 2018) was an [[Armenian-American]] chemist and [[intelligence officer]] at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]].<ref name="atomicheritage"/> He is best known for his work on high-temperature chemistry. An [[Armenian genocide]] survivor,<ref name="AP"/> he arrived in the U.S. at 4 and studied at [[Niagara University]]. He was involved in the [[Manhattan Project]]<ref name="LosAlamosSci"/> and by the time of his death was one of the last living scientists involved in it.<ref name="obit"/>

==Early life and education==
Nerses Krikorian was born in [[Harpoot|Harput]], [[Ottoman Empire]] in January 1921 to [[Armenians|Armenian]] parents Hachig and Lucy Krikorian,<ref name="manhattanprojectvoices"/> who had married in 1919.<ref name="stanford"/> The family survived the [[Armenian genocide]].<ref name="atomicheritage"/><ref name="lanl"/><ref name="manhattanprojectvoices"/> He had two brothers (Arthur and Mike), one born in [[Aleppo]], Syria and the youngest one in the U.S.<ref name="manhattanprojectvoices"/><ref name="lanl"/> and a sister, Dorothy Krikorian.<ref name="obit"/> The family fled, first, to Greece, then France, Canada and, eventually, the United States in 1925.<ref name="stanford"/> The family settled in [[Niagara Falls, New York]],<ref name="atomicheritage"/><ref name="manhattanprojectvoices"/> where his father worked in a factory, while his mother was a homemaker.<ref name="lanl"/> His parents spoke Armenian, Turkish and Kurdish, but never fully mastered English.<ref name="manhattanprojectvoices"/> He grew up in Niagara Falls and initially only spoke Armenian at the insistence of his parents. He also learned Armenian history and had knowledge of his Armenian heritage.<ref name="manhattanprojectvoices"/><ref name="lanl"/>

Krikorian studied chemistry at [[Niagara University]], a Catholic university, in 1939–43, graduating with honors.<ref name="obit"/><ref name="niagara"/><ref name="stanford"/><ref name="lanl"/>

==Career==
In 1943 Krikorian began working at an electro-metallurgical lab in [[Niagara Falls, New York|Niagara Falls]] under [[Union Carbide]] as a radiation chemist, working in a lab that made highly [[enriched uranium]] for the [[Manhattan Project]].<ref name="stanford"/><ref name="obit"/><ref name="niagara"/><ref name="lanl"/> He was initially unaware of the purpose of their work.<ref name="lanl"/><ref name="phys.org"/> "I'd read a book somewhere that speculated that uranium was a fission thing, but I didn’t know what 'fission' meant. I'm a chemist, not a physicist," Krikorian said.<ref name="lanl"/>

In August 1946 he moved to [[Los Alamos, New Mexico]] and joined [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]].<ref name="lanl"/> He began working with micrograms of highly radioactive [[polonium]]<ref name="stanford"/> to "prepare polonium-beryllium initiators."<ref name="lanl"/> In the mid-1950s he began working on [[Project Rover]], a joint project between the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|Atomic Energy Commission]] and [[NASA]], to "develop a nuclear-thermal rocket for space applications." He was responsible in ensuring that the "materials would support the rigorous demands of nuclear propulsion at high temperatures.<ref name="lanl"/><ref name="atomicheritage"/>

When Project Rover was canceled in 1972, Krikorian joined a new intelligence unit at Los Alamos National Laboratory upon the invitation of lab director [[Harold Agnew]]. He became one of the unit's six original members and its security officer. He met with representatives of the Soviet Union's nuclear research program.<ref name="atomicheritage"/> He was considered useful because he spoke Armenian and knew Russian.<ref name="lanl"/> He later became Group Leader of the Critical Technologies Group of the International Technology Division.<ref name="LosAlamosSci"/> He visited some 15 Russian laboratories, including weapons design laboratories.<ref name="LosAlamosSci"/> Krikorian was "at the forefront of dialogue between the Soviets and the United States in breaking down the barriers of the Cold War."<ref name="niagara"/>

Krikorian retired from Los Alamos National Laboratory in 1991.<ref name="lanl"/>

Krikorian helped write the charter to govern the city of [[Los Alamos, New Mexico]].<ref name="manhattanprojectvoices"/>

==Personal life and death==
Krikorian met his wife Katherine "Pat" Patterson at Los Alamos. She was a member of the [[Women's Army Corps]] (WACs) and worked as a secretary during the [[Manhattan Project]].<ref name="atomicheritage"/> They married in March 1948 and in 1951 had their only child, Debra Krikorian,<ref name="obit"/> who went on to become an army [[lieutenant colonel]].<ref name="lanl"/>

Krikorian was a founding member of the United Church of Los Alamos.<ref name="obit"/> He translated Armenian poetry and could recite the ''[[Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam|Rubaiyat]]'' of [[Omar Khayyam]].<ref name="obit"/>

He died at his home in Los Alamos on April 18, 2018<ref name="atomicheritage"/><ref name="AP"/> and was buried next to his wife at [[Santa Fe National Cemetery]].<ref name="obit"/>

==Publications==
Krikorian held six patents and authored numerous papers,<ref name="lanl"/><ref name="phys.org"/> including 50 open publications and a number of classified intelligence assessments.<ref name="obit"/> His papers were concerned with everything from [[Atomic vapor laser isotope separation|laser isotope separation]] and high-temperature reactor materials to directed-energy nuclear weapons and [[nuclear weapons testing]].<ref name="lanl"/><ref name="atomicheritage"/> He wrote on [[Rare-earth element|rare earth]] and refractory carbides, intermetallic phase relationships, [[thermodynamics]], [[crystallography]], and [[superconductivity]]. He had "developed an international reputation in high-temperature chemistry."<ref name="LosAlamosSci"/>

==Recognition==
He was named a fellow of Los Alamos National Laboratory in 1985.<ref name="obit"/> He received Los Alamos Medal, the laboratory's top medal (2003)<ref name="obit"/> and the Intelligence Community Medallion by the [[CIA]].<ref name="atomicheritage"/><ref name="lanl"/> He was awarded two honorary doctorates, from Niagara University (2005)<ref name="niagara"/> and the [[National Academy of Sciences of Armenia]] (2005).<ref>{{cite web |title=Nerses H. Krikorian |url=https://www.sci.am/membersview.php?id=356&d=1&l=27&langid=2 |website=sci.am |publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences of Armenia]] |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20191227112056/https://www.sci.am/membersview.php?id=356&d=1&l=27&langid=2 |archivedate=27 December 2019}}</ref><ref name="obit"/>

[[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] Director [[Terry Wallace (geophysicist)|Terry Wallace]] called Krikorian "a giant of national security science.<ref name="AP"/> "He contributed enormously to the mission of the laboratory [...] few people have been more impactful on our history than Krik. He leaves an enduring legacy that will continue far into the future," stated Wallace.<ref name="phys.org"/>
